issues.quote: Soon his face is blue too!
issues.problem: Present simple used for a specific future prediction. No native writer says this. It is the punchline, so learners will remember the wrong form.
issues.fix: Keep the present simple but drop the future: "It makes faces blue too. And the young man drank it!" (then cut the earlier "The young man drank it." to avoid repeating it)

notes: "He wanted to frighten the whole city." - 'frighten' is above A1; "He wanted to make the whole city afraid." is easier. This is the only real A1 vocabulary blocker, so criterion 7 passes.
A1 says Minnie saw him "from the door" while A2-C1 say "from the window". Not a contradiction a reader would notice, but "from the window" matches the other levels.

issues.quote: Soon he has a blue face too!
issues.problem: Same error as A1: present simple for a one-off future prediction is ungrammatical in English.
issues.fix: "It turns faces blue too. And our young friend drank it!"

issues.problem: This asks what amuses him in general, not why he is laughing now. It is a calque-like, unnatural question here.

notes: "He still had his house shoes on his feet." - 'slippers' is the natural British word (and the one used at B1-C1); gloss it or use "He still had his slippers on."
"Now three cabs raced across London, one behind the other." - with three cabs, "one behind another" is more natural.
"Then he walked away among the people." - "Then he walked away into the crowd." reads more naturally.

"his face went white" when he sees the tube is gone. At B1 the text never says why he chases a harmless microbe (B2 and C1 explain that it is a precious new sample). A short line such as "It was my only sample!" would close that gap.
"Follow that cab, and do not lose it!" - a shout reads better with the contraction: "don't lose it!"
"'I did, and he believed every word,' said the Bacteriologist. The Bacteriologist began to laugh again." - the name is repeated in two sentences in a row; use "He began to laugh again."
"Pour it into the water supply of London, and within a few days the sickness would be running..." - an imperative followed by 'would' is slightly mismatched; "will be running" is cleaner.
"I showed him that novelty I found last week" - 'novelty' is an odd word for a bacterium; "that new species I found last week" is closer to Wells.
"So far it has done so to a kitten..." is clunky; "So far it has turned a kitten, three puppies and a sparrow blue."
"The Bacteriologist began to laugh again" again follows straight after "said the Bacteriologist"; use "He began to laugh again."

summary: The retelling matches Wells: the anarchist-like visitor, the boast that the tube is cholera, Minnie and the coat, the three-cab chase, the swallowed drops near Waterloo Bridge and the blue-patch twist. It is suitable for 4+, and all the quizzes are keyed correctly. B1, B2 and C1 pass. A1 and A2 each fail on one ungrammatical punchline that uses the present simple for a future prediction, and A2 also has an unnatural "What makes you laugh?"; all of these are one-line fixes.
